::: {.oneline}
A response function is the rule turning a gentle push on a system into the
change it produces in something we can measure, and the frequencies at which it
becomes large are the excitations of the system itself.
:::

## Short answer

We push a system gently and watch something change. If the push is gentle
enough, the change is proportional to it (twice the push gives twice the
change), and this proportionality is the response function.

Two properties make it more than bookkeeping. First, it depends on the system
alone and not on whatever did the pushing. The same object appears whether the
push came from a laser, an electron beam or a varying magnetic field, provided
that each couples to the same property of the sample. This is why results
obtained with very different instruments can be compared at all.

Second, it respects cause and effect, since nothing changes before the push
arrives. This single fact is surprisingly powerful, since it forces the in-phase
and out-of-phase parts of the response to be tied to one another. Absorption and
refraction are therefore not independent measurements, and knowing one of them
at all frequencies determines the other.

If we push at a frequency the system likes, the response grows dramatically.
These preferred frequencies are the excitation energies of the system, and
measuring a spectrum means finding where they lie and how strongly each of them
couples to our particular kind of push.

## Why it works this way

Linear response is not an assumption about the system being simple, since the
electrons inside can interact as strongly as they like. It is an assumption
about the probe being weak enough that the excitations of the system still
organize the answer, rather than the probe reshaping the system while measuring
it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: the Kubo formula

For a perturbation $\hat H'(t) = -\hat B f(t)$ and an observable $\hat A$,
first-order perturbation theory gives

$$
\delta \langle \hat A(t)\rangle
= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dt'\; \chi_{AB}(t-t')\, f(t')
$$ {#eq-linear-response}

with the retarded response function

$$
\chi_{AB}(t-t') = -\frac{i}{\hbar}\,\theta(t-t')\,
\big\langle \big[\hat A_H(t), \hat B_H(t')\big] \big\rangle_0 .
$$ {#eq-kubo}

The commutator is what survives at first order, the step function is causality,
and the average is taken in the *unperturbed* state, which is why @eq-kubo is a
property of the system alone. Time-translation invariance of the unperturbed
Hamiltonian is what allows $\chi$ to depend on $t-t'$ only, and it is exactly
what fails out of equilibrium.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: causality and Kramers–Kronig

The step function makes $\chi(\omega)$ analytic in the upper half plane, and
contour integration then relates its real and imaginary parts,

$$
\operatorname{Re}\chi(\omega) = \frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathcal{P}\!\!
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} d\omega'\,
\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega')}{\omega' - \omega} ,
$$ {#eq-kramers-kronig}

with no model input whatsoever. As a practical consequence, an absorption
spectrum measured only up to some cutoff yields a systematically biased
refractive index.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: which operators, for optics

In the long-wavelength limit the natural pair is polarization and electric
field, so that $\chi$ is the electric susceptibility and
$\varepsilon(\omega) = 1 + \chi(\omega)$. Beyond dipole, or in the transverse
gauge, the current–current response is the natural object instead, and
translating between the two conventions is a standard source of stray factors
of $\omega$.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"The response function describes the experiment."** It describes the sample.
  The experiment only chooses which property is pushed, which one is watched,
  and with what time dependence.
- **"Its resonances are single-particle energies."** They are energies of
  *neutral* excitations, that is, differences between whole many-body states.
  This is exactly why excitons appear here and not in a band structure.
- **"Linear response is a weak-coupling theory."** It is a weak-probe theory,
  and says nothing about how strongly the constituents interact with each other.
